**_Building a High-Performance AI Backed API: Scaling To Thousands of Inferences Per Second_**

Press enter or click to view image in full size

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/0*IMZc2xM8pt71Vk_k)

At [ActiveFence](https://www.activefence.com/), our mission is to protect online platforms and their users from various harms and abuses. In this post, we’ll share key lessons learned from scaling our architecture and infrastructure to meet the demands of high throughput and low latency model inference.

As if building an API for content moderation that supports many media types and is backed by high-accuracy models, was not challenging enough, at the beginning of 2024, we faced a new challenge: our API needed to support real-time moderation on chat messages, allowing platforms to filter abusive content before it was published. This synchronous text API had to handle tens of thousands of analyses per second while maintaining extremely low latency.

Like any major project, we needed a clear strategy to meet our goals on time. But before we could map out our gaps and build a roadmap, to achieve them, we needed to ensure we had reliable metrics. These would not only enable us to identify gaps but also for evaluating our progress and determining if we met our success criteria.

## Metrics and Evaluation

We recognized the need to reduce the end-to-end latency of ActiveScore (our content moderation API) by 80%, while supporting a constant rate of 400% to 500% increase relative to our previous throughput. Establishing measurable metrics before testing is important to avoid falling into mental traps such as the [confirmation bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confirmation_bias), which can lead to misinterpreting the results in a way that validates prior beliefs. By defining these metrics and their meaning in advance, we can ensure we adhere to absolute facts while we track our success in achieving our goals.

Before diving into performance improvements, we had to first clearly define our service level objectives (SLOs), or what latency and error rates our system could tolerate over what time intervals. Specifically, _p95 < x_ measured over one hour interval is a different requirement than if it is measured over one month. Once we agreed on these targets with our product and customer success teams, we could start planning how to measure them.

Some application observability vendors report timers using gauges, which aggregated at the agent level before sending the metrics to the observability platform backend. Meaning, if your application is running in a container orchestration system like Kubernetes, and each application instance emits a latency timer, those timers are likely aggregated at the host level (like EC2). As a result you might see metrics like _my\_route\_timer.avg, my\_route\_timer.max, my\_route\_timer.95percentile_.

However, these metrics don’t allow for proper monitoring of the overall application’s 95 percentile, because probabilistic metrics are not additive. When calculating percentiles, you’re determining a ranking position within a specific dataset. If you were to add two percentile vectors, you would break this ranking relationship. This means you could miss the impact of outliers on overall latency. To mitigate this, we decided to emit raw latency histograms and ensure they were not aggregated at any container, pod, or node level before being shipped to the metrics backend system. This approach allows us to monitor raw latency data across the entire application.

## The cost of fan-out

Another example that highlights the importance of setting the right measurements involves a high-level understanding of our architecture. When a client makes a request to our API, we first fetch the account configuration to determine which AI models should run for that request. We then fan out n requests to those models:

Understanding how this “fan out” impacts end-to-end latency is crucial for making sure we are looking at the right metrics. A request end to end latency will be determined by the slowest model’s processing time. Since each model’s latency operates independently, for the request latency to be under X milliseconds, each model must also have a processing time of less than X milliseconds (for simplicity, we’re neglecting the API component processing time).

In formula terms, to obtain accurate metrics for model execution, we need to look at the p99 latency (for clients having five models configured) of the model service, even though we are primarily interested in the p95 latency for end-to-end monitoring. You can see the mathematical reason in the formula below, but intuitively this is because the combination of independent probabilities is simply their multiplication, so _p(0.99)⁵ is p(0.95)_.

## Building Our Strategy

Once we implemented proper measurements and could clearly track our progress and success, as well as creating the right indicators in our observability vendor platform for easy identification of potential bottlenecks (i.e. dashboards focused on the right metrics), we ran a test to assess the gap from our initial milestone of 5,000 requests per seconds with a latency of less than 180 ms in our testing environment.

The test was quite naive — we started at the target requests per second with random inputs in a testing environment, and unsurprisingly, it failed miserably: latency kept growing while having more failures than successes. Auto-scaling for services wasn’t properly tuned for the target latency, which meant the services couldn’t maintain predictable SLOs for the requests they could handle.

We realized we needed a better strategy to tackle this challenge. Our approach consisted of three main steps:

1. Identifying algorithmic and topological bottlenecks.
2. Shortening the long tail latencies that were raising our high percentiles.
3. Reducing waste to ensure our system operated as efficiently as possible.

## Getting it Done

### Identifying algorithmic and topological bottlenecks

To identify bottlenecks, we ran a test with unlimited resources. This way we know that resource limitations cannot be the root cause of high latency. This wasn’t a load or stress test. We ensured that every component had more than enough CPU cores and each model had sufficient GPU accessible to it to handle the test workloads (Memory and I/O were not a limiting resource for our use case). The test revealed that some models lagged behind others, leading us to change their underlying infrastructure and to [quantize](https://huggingface.co/docs/optimum/en/concept_guides/quantization#quantization) them.

### Shortening the long tail latencies

Once we were satisfied with the performance of a single request without resource limitations, we moved to addressing our target goal of end-to-end p95 latency with less than 180 ms. We realized that we now faced a probability problem: not all requests could be served under 180 ms or even 500 ms. Software occasionally has hiccups, for example due to sharing machines between different agents, Kubernetes operations, etc. These are unavoidable and out of our control. However, we could reduce their impact by reducing I/O operations and implementing proper load balancing.

**Batching Requests**

To reduce the impact of fanning out requests (described above), we batched requests to the same microservice. While this increased the overall time it took for the microservice to handle a request, it reduced the impact of any single model slowing down the entire request (instead of waiting for the slowest out of over 30 requests, we only waited for one, decreasing the chances of hitting a network hiccups for incoming API requests).

**Local Caching**

We pulled account configuration data from Redis upon each request. By caching it on each application instance memory, we removed redundant calls to Redis, which could occasionally affect long-tail latencies. While most Redis calls took less than 3 ms, some could take up to 100 ms. Given that our account configuration is mostly static, in-memory caching even for just one minute significantly reduced the network toll when serving 10,000 requests per second.

**Load Balancing**

Usually Kubernetes pod-to-pod communication is done using a ClusterIP. From the [docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/cluster-ip-allocation/):

> “In Kubernetes, Services are an abstract way to expose an application running on a set of Pods. Services can have a cluster-scoped virtual IP address (using a Service of type: ClusterIP). Clients can connect using that virtual IP address, and Kubernetes then load-balances traffic to that Service across the different backing Pods.”

But as we discovered, for applications communicating using HTTP at large scales and with auto-scaling, this may be far from ideal.

**Decentralized**

When client pod A interacts with backend pod B using the service’s ClusterIP DNS, CoreDNS handles the DNS resolution, returning the ClusterIP for the service. This ClusterIP is virtual and doesn’t point to any specific pod directly. Instead, traffic directed to the ClusterIP is intercepted by kube-proxy on the client node. kube-proxy then performs NAT (Network Address Translation) to map the ClusterIP to the IP of one of the backend pods.

kube-proxy maintains iptable rules on each node that map service ClusterIPs to the available backend pod IPs. Load balancing is handled at the node level, meaning the traffic distribution happens without coordination between nodes. If your client application is running across multiple nodes, the load balancing remains isolated on each node, which can lead to uneven traffic distribution — especially when scaling, as kube-proxy on one node is unaware of the load on pods that are being targeted by requests from other nodes.

**Load Balancing Algorithm**

The load balancing at the node level is essentially random selection from the service’s backend pods iptable. Meaning that as long as the pod is healthy from k8s perspective, it may receive new requests to handle regardless of other factors that may impact its latency (like the amount of in-flight requests).

**TCP Level Load Balancing**

Once a pod IP is returned to the application for connection establishment, there’s not much room for optimizations. You could maintain a keep-alive mechanism, which can hinder scaling as new pods may not receive requests as desired. Alternatively, closing connections after each request comes with making a handshake for each request toll. Plus, if connections are kept alive, this is managed by your HTTP client at layer 4 (TCP), while the applications communicate at layer 7 (HTTP). Meaning, there’s no limitation on the amount of HTTP requests sent on the same open connections by default, which is likely to harm your load balancing.

Those problems can be solved in various ways, from client side load balancing (which requires service discovery and proper connection management with HTTP factors in it) to service mesh solutions. While both are likely to help us achieve our goal, we decided to use AWS ALB — a managed load balancer which addresses all of the above challenges:

1. It is centralized which helps maximize its load balancing potential
2. It supports multiple load balancing algorithms such as [Least Outstanding Requests](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2019/11/application-load-balancer-now-supports-least-outstanding-requests-algorithm-for-load-balancing-requests/)
3. It supports “IP mode” enabling connection management with the target groups (backend pods) directly.

## Making it Efficient as Possible

After overcoming these challenges, we successfully met our SLOs. Our p95 latencies and error rates were both below target. Importantly, we achieved this without imposing any resource limits. At this point, we turned our attention to improving resource utilization.

Resource utilization improvement can also be described as reducing waste. The resources to optimize for a given application are:

- CPU
- Memory
- Network sockets/connections
- GPU (for GPU-based models)

Any underutilized resource on that list indicates waste. Improving utilization can be achieved by either adjusting the provisioned resources or improving the application behavior/code to reduce other resource consumption until utilization is satisfying .

While the details of our resource optimization is beyond this post’s scope, we found the event loop lag metric invaluable for assessing application health. Event loop lag measures the time it takes for a scheduled task to start its execution. For instance, if a task scheduled at time T starts its execution at T + 5,the event loop lag would be 5, indicating that something else held the CPU during that time and this task could not be executed.This metric helped us for example surface painful garbage collection operations that affected our long-tail latency and application instance throughput, which we addressed by improving code quality and reducing amounts of objects creation. By doing that, we were able to reduce the “stop-the-world” garbage collection cycles.

## Summary

In this post, we shared our journey of enhancing our content moderation API, ActiveScore, to handle tens of thousands of requests per second with sub-second latency for pre-publishing content moderation. Initially, we focused on establishing reliable metrics to gauge the performance improvements needed to meet strict SLOs. This involved redefining our latency and error rate targets and implementing precise, measurable metrics.

As we progressed, we addressed both probabilistic challenges and utilization challenges. This strategic approach not only helped us meet our initial performance targets but also set the foundation for ongoing improvements and scalability. The insights gained from this experience underscore the importance of proper planning, continuous monitoring, and proactive optimization in managing high-performance APIs at scale.
